::: {.lead}
Coding agents can fix many small, well-specified issues, but people still sit and watch them, because a run that dies loses its work and a run that loops quietly burns money. Longhaul is the harness that makes an agent safe to leave alone. It takes a GitHub issue, works on it for hours in a sandbox, resumes where it stopped after a crash, and asks a person only at checkpoints. It ends with a pull request or an honest report of where it got stuck.
:::

## The problem

Teams have a long tail of small, well-specified issues: a bug with a clear repro, a missing flag, a test that fails after a dependency bump. Run by hand in a terminal, an agent fails in five predictable ways.

::: {.failure-list}
1. **Runs die.** A laptop sleeps, a container is killed, the API returns 529 for ten minutes. The agent loses its state and pays for the same tokens twice.
2. **Context fills up.** A long task overflows the context window. The agent forgets what it already tried and loops.
3. **Nobody knows it is stuck.** The agent keeps editing the same three lines for forty minutes. Cost climbs and nobody is told.
4. **Side effects repeat.** A retry posts the same comment twice or opens a second pull request.
5. **Cost is a surprise.** With no per-task budget and no ledger, the bill is the first signal.
:::

## How it works

A poller finds the issues that carry the `longhaul` label and starts one Temporal workflow for each. The workflow only decides what runs next. Each model turn, tool call, checkpoint and write to GitHub is an activity of its own, so when a worker dies, Temporal retries that one step from the last checkpoint and the task goes on.

::: {.diagram-fit}
```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-overview
%%| column: page
%%| fig-cap: "The life of one task. The architecture page has the system context and every step of the workflow."
flowchart LR
  ISSUE(["Issue labeled<br/>longhaul"]) --> PLAN["Planner reads the repo<br/>and posts a plan"]
  PLAN -->|approved, when the<br/>repo asks for it| CODE["Coder works in turns:<br/>model turn, tool call,<br/>git checkpoint"]
  CODE -->|finish| VERIFY["Verifier runs the tests<br/>and reviews the diff"]
  VERIFY -->|send back| CODE
  VERIFY -->|pass| PR(["Pull request<br/>with a run report"])
  CODE -->|stuck or<br/>out of budget| PAUSE["Pause and ask<br/>one question"]
  PAUSE -->|hint or top-up| CODE
  VERIFY -->|fails 3 times| STUCK(["Report of where<br/>it got stuck"])
  PAUSE -->|no answer in time| STUCK
```
:::

A person steers from the issue (`/longhaul approve`, `hint`, `budget`, `cancel`) or from the console, and the agent writes to GitHub through one module with an idempotency key, so a retry never posts twice.

Four ideas carry it.

::: {.idea-grid}
::: {.idea}
**Durable turns.** Every model turn and every tool call is its own Temporal activity, with its own timeout, retry and heartbeat. A worker that dies loses one step and not the task.
:::

::: {.idea}
**Git checkpoints.** Every change in the workspace is a commit in a bare repo per task. A retried tool call starts from its `pre_sha`, so it never runs on half-applied edits.
:::

::: {.idea}
**Two-tier context.** Old tool outputs shrink to a one-line stub with a handle, and older turns become structured progress notes, so a task of a hundred turns fits the window.
:::

::: {.idea}
**Plan, verify, stuck.** A planner, a coder and a verifier work inside one workflow. A stuck detector pauses the run and asks one specific question, and hard budgets stop the spend.
:::
:::

Around them: a hardened Docker sandbox with no credentials inside, a cost ledger with a row for every model call, a memory that only a merged pull request or a person can write to, traces, metrics, and a console. The agent never pushes to a default branch, and a person merges every pull request. The [architecture page](architecture.qmd) shows how the pieces connect, and the [decisions page](decisions.qmd) records why they were chosen.

## The proof

The chaos suite puts a number behind "survives crashes". It ran four recorded tasks 20 times, and each run was given one to three kills of the worker, the sandbox, Temporal or Postgres, timed to land while the task works. Every run ended with a pull request and the same diff as a run with no kill, and the fake GitHub that each run wrote to showed no duplicate and no missing write.

::: {fragment="_generated/chaos-chart.md"}
:::

::: {fragment="_generated/chaos-table.md"}
:::

The model answers in these runs were scripted recordings, so the suite measures durability and not how well a model codes. The [results page](results.qmd) explains each column, the limits, and the model evaluation that is still to run. The [gate reports](gates.qmd) hold the evidence that each phase is done, including what failed and what was fixed.

## The console

A person watches every task, reads its timeline turn by turn, and steps in from the console: approve a plan, send a hint, add budget or cancel. These screenshots come from the demo stack, which runs the scripted provider, so every cost on them is $0.00.

## Try it

You need Docker, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and Python 3.12. No API key and no GitHub account are needed: the scripted provider plays a fixed set of model answers.

```bash
git clone {{< meta source-repo >}}.git
cd longhaul-autonomous-coding-agent-github
make setup && make up && make demo
```

`make demo` runs one task on a small package whose `add()` subtracts, prints each status line and the final diff, and stops. To run Longhaul on your own repo, follow "Run on your repo" in the [README]({{< meta source-repo >}}#run-on-your-repo) and the [runbook](runbook.qmd).

## Where it stands

The table is read from the [progress page](progress.qmd) each time the site is built. Phase 0 has two stories open, and both wait on steps the owner takes on GitHub: branch protection for `dev` and `main`, and the import of the backlog as issues. The [Phase 0 gate report](gates.qmd#phase-0-gate-foundation-and-backlog-import) has the details.
